"Score the card 1-5 on each criterion. For each score give ref, the card line (card:<field>) that decides it, or plan:<field path> when no card line carries it, and a reason of at most 25 words. Use NA only where a criterion allows it. Then name decides_by: the id of the earliest phase after which decision_rule can be applied whichever outcome occurs, or \"none\". A phase that only reproduces a published number, or only measures throughput the question does not ask about, does not count. Give decides_by_reason in at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Root question: What limits Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models for river catchments, which needs long MCMC chains? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could that be fixed with a shit ton of GPU parallelism?
Option record: {\"id\":\"Large-sample multi-catchment calibration\",\"title\":\"Large-sample multi-catchment calibration (CAMELS)\",\"summary\":\"Calibrating many catchments (CAMELS provides 671 US catchments) is embarrassingly parallel because each catchment is independently calibratable, so GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization.\",\"root_link\":\"Bears on the \\"whether a shit ton of GPUs fixes it\\" half — at CAMELS scale, throughput determines how many catchments can be afforded full Bayesian treatment.\",\"compute_open\":\"More parallel compute buys catchments given full Bayesian treatment instead of point optimization; the largest published set is CAMELS's 671 US catchments (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html), and it is still unknown what extending full Bayesian treatment to all catchments above 671 (or globally) would change about large-sample hydrological conclusions.\",\"sequential\":\"none — the catchments are independently calibratable, so the study already splits into one independent calibration per catchment (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html).\",\"source_urls\":[\"https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html\",\"https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305\"]}
Card:
card:question: Does GPU parallelism change how many of the 671 CAMELS catchments can get full Bayesian calibration instead of point optimization?
card:hypothesis: Each catchment calibrates independently, so GPU batching turns full Bayesian treatment of all 671 into a cheap throughput problem, not a blocker.
card:sequential_part: Each catchment's posterior waits on one chain's 100,000 serial proposal-accept steps; four chains per catchment.
card:method: none - the 671 catchments' four chains each are independent, so all 2,684 chains run side by side in one batched pass.
card:if_lever: One GPU gives >=20x over CPU and finishes all 671 in under an hour, so compute is the lever here.
card:if_not: Vectorized CPU finishes all 671 in a couple of hours, so throughput does not decide which catchments get full Bayesian treatment.
card:test_summary: Time full Bayesian MCMC (4 chains x 1e5 iterations, R-hat<1.2) for 671 CAMELS catchments on one GPU versus a vectorized CPU and versus point optimization; measure whether GPU throughput decides how many catchments get full Bayesian treatment.
card:closest_prior: Freitas et al. 2022 GPU-optimized a hydrological model's calibration to 20x CPU speedup, on one distributed model, not batched MCMC across many GR4J catchments [s_mgb].
card:left_open: No published result times batched GPU MCMC giving all 671 CAMELS catchments full Bayesian GR4J treatment, so the crossover is unmeasured [s_mgb].
card:anchor: Reproduce airGR's GR4J: parameter set X=(165.05, 6.46, 422.50, 2.45) gives calibration NSE 0.495 on its example basin [s_airgr_nse].
card:limits: Shows GR4J only, not expensive distributed or hierarchical models; US CAMELS unless the optional global stretch runs; nothing about single-chain mixing limits.

Criteria:
stakes: Take the two outcomes this test predicts, as measured here and within the limits in scope_gap. 5 = whichever occurs, a choice someone faces (what to buy, build, collect or scale next) changes, and the test measures the quantity that choice depends on; 3 = the outcomes bear on that choice only through a step this test does not check (a stand-in system, simulation to reality, a single model), or one outcome is already much more likely than the other; 1 = neither outcome would change anything. Do not score how famous the field is or how close it is to the root question.
lever: Could the result tell if_lever from if_not, with compute the only thing that changed? Check four conditions: (a) the predicted difference between if_lever and if_not is larger than what noise_rule says run-to-run noise can produce; (b) compute_axis spans at least 10×; (c) the varied quantity is bought with compute, not with more data, labels or people (when restructuring.method is not none: the arms run on the same hardware and differ only in method); (d) inputs that could also explain the difference are in held_fixed. 5 = all four hold; 3 = one fails or cannot be told from the plan; 1 = two or more fail, or the measured quantity is not the one the question asks about.
verifiable: What is the measured outcome scored against? 5 = an exact or planted truth that does not come from the method under test (a simulation's hidden true run, an exact success flag, a formal checker, planted items), and the setup first reproduces a published number within a stated tolerance; 3 = labels from a model or human rater with an agreement check, or exact truth with no reproduction step; 1 = nothing independent of the method's own output.
open: Does the closest published result already answer this question over this range? 5 = the quoted prior stops short of this range or asks a different question, and the plan states the gap; 3 = the prior answers part of it (a narrower range, a related system), or no prior is named; 1 = the quoted prior already answers it. Reusing published tools, models or benchmarks does not lower this score.
reshape: Does the plan remove a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on, rather than run independent work side by side? 5 = restructuring names the dependency, why it need not run in order and how the plan computes it at the same time; condition says what must hold for that to pay off; condition_phase measures it before the main spend; and the closest prior does not already do this for this system; 3 = it removes a dependency, but condition is missing or is not measured before the main spend; 2 = it parallelises only within each step (splitting a large state across GPUs) or regroups and rebalances independent work (batching unfinished runs, load balancing, lower precision), leaving the chain in order; 1 = independent copies side by side, or one job per GPU, is the only parallelism, or the plan rebuilds a parallel version the closest prior already reports for this system. Reusing a method published for a different system does not lower this score.
baseline: Is the gain timed against the strongest ways to get the same answer without the plan's method? Check four conditions: (a) baseline_sequential is tuned (compiled, vectorised or multithreaded code, or a published optimised code), not a plain interpreted loop; (b) baseline_copies is timed on the same GPUs; (c) anchor checks the parallel result against the sequential one within a stated tolerance; (d) a named phase times every arm as time or dollars to one answer, so the gain is measured, not only modelled. 5 = all four hold; 3 = one fails or cannot be told from the plan; 1 = two or more fail. NA when restructuring.method is none.

Let me score each criterion.

Stakes: Two outcomes: if_lever (GPU <1hr, ≥20x) vs if_not. If if_lever, compute is the lever — buy GPUs; if_not, throughput doesn't decide, so fall back... Actually the choice changing: whether to buy GPU compute to give all 671 catchments Bayesian treatment. But scope: within limits — GR4J only. The choice at stake: what to buy/build next. The card's if_not says "throughput does not decide which catchments get full Bayesian treatment" — that's a bit odd. The decision: invest in GPU vs point optimization. Scores ~4? Limits say single model, stand-in — criterion says 3 = outcomes bear on choice only through a step not checked (a single model). The scope_gap mentions only cheap GR4J, so it's a single model. But the actual choice (buy GPU for CAMELS-scale Bayesian calibration) is directly measured... though generalizing to expensive distributed models is a step not checked. I'd give 4. Hmm, but the criterion says 3 = "bear on that choice only through a step this test does not check (a stand-in system, ... a single model)". The choice "what to buy next" for GR4J CAMELS calibration is directly measured. But the root question is broader (rainfall-runoff models generally). Within scope, the choice is which catchments get full Bayesian treatment — the test measures that directly. I'll say 4: choice (buy GPU vs fall back to point optimization) changes, directly measured, but only one cheap model within limits.

Lever: (a) predicted difference: if_lever <1hr GPU with ≥20x vs if_not vectorized CPU couple hours. Noise <5%, difference 20x — yes. (b) compute_axis spans 67/335/671 = 10x. Yes exactly 10x. (c) varied quantity bought with compute: restructuring.method is "none" — arms differ... arm_gpu vs arm_cpu differ by hardware (GPU vs CPU), which is compute. But wait, condition (c): "when restructuring.method is not none: the arms run on same hardware and differ only in method". Here method is none, so arms: GPU vs vectorized CPU — compute is the only thing changed (same sampler). (d) inputs in held_fixed: yes — chains, iterations, GR4J, record, likelihood, hardware. But note: the decision_rule includes "GPU beats vectorized CPU by ≥20x AND <1hr". Is CPU3 hours a GUESS — measured by gpu_bench. Hmm, cpu_baseline phase times it. The20x threshold comes from a proxy (s_mgb, different model, point calibration) — differs_in acknowledged. Does that fail (a)? The difference between if_lever and if_not: if_lever is <1hr and ≥20x. If GPU gives 5x, if_not. Noise <5%. So distinguishable. I'd give 5... but potential issue: decision_rule "GPU <1hr AND ≥20x" — combined conditions, both measured directly. I'll give 5. Actually wait — is the measured quantity the one the question asks about? The root question: "could compute be fixed with GPU parallelism?" Yes, wall-clock + speedup is that quantity. Give 5.

Hmm, but one concern: compute_axis levels 67/335/671 spans 10x exactly — condition (b) "at least 10×" holds.

Verifiable: anchor = airGR NSE 0.495 published number within ±0.02 tolerance, reproduction step. Measured outcome: wall-clock time — scored against what? The decision rule uses thresholds (1 hour, 20x) — those are thresholded measurements, not exact truth. Verifiable criterion: "What is the measured outcome scored against? 5 = exact or planted truth... and setup first reproduces a published number within stated tolerance; 3 = ... exact truth with no reproduction; 1 = nothing independent." The measured outcome is timing — timing is measured directly (deterministic-ish), but the scored-against for correctness: R-hat<1.2, anchor NSE 0.495 published. There is a reproduction step (airGR NSE 0.495 ±0.02). The timing isn't scored against truth but against thresholds — but wall-clock is directly measurable. I'd say 5: anchor reproduces published number within tolerance, plus checks against airGR simulation within 1%. Ref: card:anchor.

Open: closest prior Freitas et al. 2022 — GPU 20x on one distributed model, point calibration, not batched MCMC across catchments; card:left_open states gap. 5.

Reshape: Does the plan remove a step-after-step dependency? restructuring: sequential_part names dependency (each catchment's chain serial 1e5 steps), method says none — runs all chains in parallel. But this is "independent copies side by side" — embarrassingly parallel across catchments. Condition for reshape 5: names dependency, why it need not run in order, computes simultaneously; condition (if_lever/if_not?) measures it before main spend — gpu_bench measures batched throughput before main run. But criterion: 2 = parallelises only within each step or regroups independent work... 1 = "independent copies side by side, or one job per GPU, is the only parallelism". Here the parallelism is exactly independent chains side by side — one batched pass. The dependency named is within-chain serial steps (proposal-accept) which is NOT removed — chains still run 1e5 serial steps. The restructuring just runs independent chains concurrently. That's independent copies side by side → score 1? Hmm. But card:sequential_part names a dependency: "Each catchment's posterior waits on one chain's 100,000 serial proposal-accept steps". method: none — run all side by side.
